items.sentence: The new timetable will ___ every Year 10 class.
items.explanation: 'Affect' is usually the verb: to influence something.

items.sentence: Lack of sleep had a noticeable ___ on her revision.
items.explanation: 'Effect' is usually the noun: a result. Tip: Affect is the Action, Effect is the End result.

items.sentence: You need to ___ your presentation before Friday.
items.explanation: In British English, 'practise' with an s is the verb.

items.sentence: Regular ___ makes new vocabulary stick.
items.explanation: 'Practice' with a c is the noun. 'Advice' (noun) and 'advise' (verb) follow the same pattern.

items.sentence: You'll need a valid driving ___ to hire the van.
items.explanation: British English: 'licence' is the noun.

items.sentence: The council will only ___ two new food stalls this year.
items.explanation: British English: 'license' is the verb. (American English uses 'license' for both.)

items.sentence: Could you ___ me on which module to choose?
items.explanation: 'Advise' (with an s, said with a z sound) is the verb.

items.sentence: Thanks for the ___; I'll take it on board.
items.explanation: 'Advice' (with a c) is the noun, and it's uncountable: 'some advice', never 'an advice'.

items.sentence: The chutney is the perfect ___ to a strong cheddar.
items.explanation: A 'complement' completes something or goes well with it. Think 'complete'.

items.sentence: She paid me a lovely ___ about my presentation.
items.explanation: A 'compliment' is praise. Think 'I like it'.

items.sentence: On ___, I don't answer work emails at weekends.
items.explanation: A 'principle' is a rule or belief.

items.sentence: The ___ reason for the delay was a supplier issue.
items.explanation: 'Principal' means main. It's also the head of some colleges.

items.sentence: Traffic was ___ on the M25 for over an hour.
items.explanation: 'Stationary' means not moving.

items.sentence: The staffroom has run out of ___ again: pens, paper, the lot.
items.explanation: 'Stationery' is writing materials. Tip: stationEry is for Envelopes.

items.sentence: There were ___ students in the lecture than last week.
items.explanation: Use 'fewer' with things you can count: students, emails, biscuits.

items.sentence: I've got ___ time than I thought.
items.explanation: Use 'less' with things you can't count: time, money, water.

items.sentence: Are you trying to ___ that I'm always late?
items.explanation: The speaker implies (suggests) something.

items.sentence: From the data, we can ___ that the trend will continue.
items.explanation: The listener or reader infers (concludes) something.

items.sentence: Please be ___: the restructure isn't public yet.
items.explanation: 'Discreet' means careful to keep things private.

items.sentence: The course is split into six ___ modules.
items.explanation: 'Discrete' means separate and distinct, as in maths: discrete data.

items.sentence: Use open questions to ___ ideas from the class.
items.explanation: To 'elicit' is to draw out a response.

items.sentence: Trading Standards seized hundreds of ___ copies of the game.
items.explanation: 'Illicit' means illegal or forbidden.

items.sentence: Please ___ that all laptops are locked away before you leave.
items.explanation: To 'ensure' is to make sure.

items.sentence: It costs a fortune to ___ a car for a new driver.
items.explanation: To 'insure' is to take out insurance.

items.sentence: The final grade is ___ on the coursework.
items.explanation: 'Dependent' (with -ent) is the adjective.

items.sentence: You can add a ___ to your health insurance policy.
items.explanation: In British English, a 'dependant' (with -ant) is a person, often a child, who relies on you financially.

items.sentence: The local ___ is finally fixing the potholes.
items.explanation: A 'council' is an elected body, like your local council.

items.sentence: She sought legal ___ before signing the contract.
items.explanation: 'Counsel' is advice, or a barrister in court.

items.sentence: A referee must be completely ___.
items.explanation: 'Disinterested' means impartial: with nothing to gain.

items.sentence: He looked thoroughly ___ in the cricket.
items.explanation: 'Uninterested' means not interested or bored.

items.sentence: The ___ interruptions made it impossible to concentrate.
items.explanation: 'Continual' means happening again and again, with breaks.

items.sentence: The spring provides a ___ supply of water.
items.explanation: 'Continuous' means without any break at all.

items.sentence: The ___ outlook for next year is uncertain.
items.explanation: 'Economic' relates to the economy.

items.sentence: Buying in bulk is far more ___.
items.explanation: 'Economical' means good value, not wasteful.

items.sentence: Winning the league was a ___ moment for the club.
items.explanation: 'Historic' means important in history.

items.sentence: The drama is based on ___ records from the 1600s.
items.explanation: 'Historical' means about or from the past.

items.sentence: Don't ___ your train ticket; the inspector's on board.
items.explanation: 'Lose' (one o) means to misplace or fail to win.

items.sentence: This screw has come ___ again.
items.explanation: 'Loose' (two o's) means not tight.

items.sentence: Better lighting should ___ the risk of falls.
items.explanation: To 'mitigate' is to make something less severe.

items.sentence: Several factors ___ against an early launch.
items.explanation: To 'militate against' is to work against something. It's almost always followed by 'against'.

items.sentence: Shouting will only ___ the problem.
items.explanation: To 'exacerbate' is to make a situation worse.

items.sentence: His constant excuses really ___ me.
items.explanation: To 'exasperate' is to annoy a person intensely.

items.sentence: We'll ___ the old API next quarter and remove it in the spring.
items.explanation: To 'deprecate' a feature is to mark it as outdated.

items.sentence: New cars ___ quickly in their first year.
items.explanation: To 'depreciate' is to lose value over time.

items.sentence: The revision guide is ___: it covers every topic on the syllabus.
items.explanation: 'Comprehensive' means including everything.

items.sentence: Her explanation was clear and ___, even to complete beginners.
items.explanation: 'Comprehensible' means understandable.

items.sentence: The instructions were ___: they could be read two ways.
items.explanation: 'Ambiguous' describes something with more than one possible meaning.

items.sentence: I'm ___ about the move: excited, but sad to leave.
items.explanation: 'Ambivalent' describes mixed feelings.

items.sentence: The link between the two events is ___ at best.
items.explanation: 'Tenuous' means weak or flimsy.

items.sentence: We've made a ___ booking for Saturday, just in case.
items.explanation: 'Tentative' means provisional, not yet certain.

items.sentence: She was able to ___ the claim with hard evidence.
items.explanation: To 'refute' a claim is to prove it wrong.

items.sentence: He continues to ___ the allegations, but offers no proof.
items.explanation: To 'deny' something is just to say it isn't true. Using 'refute' here would claim he'd proved it.

items.sentence: After last time, he's ___ to lend anyone money.
items.explanation: 'Reluctant to do something' means unwilling.

items.sentence: She's quite ___ about her personal life at work.
items.explanation: 'Reticent' means reserved, not revealing much. Strictly, it isn't followed by 'to do'.

items.sentence: The committee ___ eight members.
items.explanation: 'Comprise' doesn't take 'of'. If you want 'of', use 'consists of' or 'is made up of'.

items.sentence: Could you ___ me a fiver until Friday?
items.explanation: You lend something to someone.

items.sentence: Can I ___ your charger for a minute?
items.explanation: You borrow something from someone. 'Can you borrow me…' is a common regional slip.

items.sentence: Some drivers ___ the 20 mph limit outside the school.
items.explanation: To 'flout' a rule is to openly break it.

items.sentence: If you've got it, ___ it.
items.explanation: To 'flaunt' is to show off.

items.sentence: I'm not ___ to a bit of overtime before Christmas.
items.explanation: 'Averse to' describes a person's dislike: 'risk-averse'.

items.sentence: The trial was paused after several ___ reactions.
items.explanation: 'Adverse' means harmful or unfavourable: 'adverse weather'.

items.sentence: We visit my parents on ___ weekends.
items.explanation: In British English, 'alternate' means every other one.

items.sentence: Is there an ___ route if the bridge is closed?
items.explanation: In British English, another option is an 'alternative'. American English often says 'alternate' here.

items.sentence: An ___ historian will open the conference.
items.explanation: 'Eminent' means famous and respected.

items.sentence: Rain is ___: bring the washing in!
items.explanation: 'Imminent' means about to happen.

items.sentence: It's ___ good, actually. I wasn't expecting much.
items.explanation: 'Quite' (ends -ite) means fairly, or completely.

items.sentence: Could you keep it ___? The baby's finally asleep.
items.explanation: 'Quiet' (ends -et) means not noisy.

items.sentence: I'm ___ to admit it, but you were right.
items.explanation: 'Loath' (no e) is an adjective: reluctant.

items.sentence: I ___ queuing in the rain.
items.explanation: 'Loathe' (with an e) is a verb: to hate.

items.sentence: She spent the whole evening ___ over the data.
items.explanation: To 'pore over' something is to study it closely.

items.sentence: Take a brolly: it's ___ down out there.
items.explanation: 'Pouring' (with a u) is about liquid, including heavy rain.

items.sentence: Nothing seems to ___ her, not even an Ofsted visit.
items.explanation: To 'faze' someone is to unsettle them.

items.sentence: We'll ___ in the changes over the spring term.
items.explanation: To 'phase in' is to introduce something in stages.

items.sentence: The ___ review happens every January and July.
items.explanation: 'Biannual' means twice a year.

items.sentence: The festival is ___, so the next one is in two years' time.
items.explanation: 'Biennial' means every two years.

items.sentence: Bring something warm, ___ a jumper or a fleece.
items.explanation: 'E.g.' means for example: one of several possibilities.

items.sentence: The deadline is the last day of term, ___ Friday 18 December.
items.explanation: 'I.e.' means that is: it pins down exactly what you mean.
